args.title: arbitration-markup-analysis-memo.docx
args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
MEMORANDUM
To: Engaged Client; Deal Team
From: Legal — Arbitration International Dispute Resolution
Re: Analysis of Counterparty Markup of Arbitration Agreement — Accept / Reject / Counter Recommendations
Date: [Matter Date]

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This memorandum analyzes the counterparty's redline markup of our arbitration agreement (the "Counterparty Markup") against the governing base materials — the original draft arbitration agreement, the relevant stock purchase agreement ("SPA") excerpts, the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and the internal deal-team playbook — and sets forth accept/reject/counter recommendations for each deviation introduced by the counterparty.

The Counterparty Markup accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three material deviations:
(1) a silent reduction of the indemnification cap and a conversion of the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket;
(2) new carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") targeting regulatory action of precisely the kind at issue in this matter; and
(3) a new limitation period that shortens survival of the core representations.

Each deviation is reconciled below against the SPA excerpts, the disclosure schedules (Schedule 3.7 and Schedule 5.2), Exhibit B (survival matrix), and the controlling instructions from the deal team.

II. GOVERNING FRAMEWORK AND CONTROLLING INSTRUCTIONS

A. Disclosure Schedules Control. The disclosure schedules qualify the base materials. Schedule 3.7 and Schedule 5.2, together with Exhibit B, narrow the very representations that the Counterparty Markup also touches. As the base materials make express, "scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base arbitration international dispute resolution materials." Accordingly, the analysis in this memo treats each scheduled exception as controlling where it overlaps a markup change.

B. Controlling Deal-Team Instruction. The deal-team correspondence contains an email thread on this engagement. The latest message REVISES the analysis priorities: the client will CONCEDE the basket conversion but treats any SURVIVAL-PERIOD REDUCTION as a WALK-AWAY ISSUE. Only the latest message controls; earlier messages stating the opposite ordering are superseded. This memo implements the controlling instruction.

C. Excluded Material. An administrative correspondence file was misfiled into the matter folder concerning a different engagement. It is a distractor and is disregarded in this analysis.

III. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

DEVIATION 1 — Indemnification: Silent Reduction of the Cap; Conversion of the Basket from a Deductible to a Tipping Basket

What the Markup Does. The counterparty silently reduces the indemnification cap and converts the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket.

Analysis.
• Basket Conversion (deductible → tipping). Under a deductible basket, the buyer bears the risk of loss below the threshold and recovery applies only above it; under a tipping basket, once the threshold is crossed the entire loss is recoverable. Conversion to a tipping basket generally favors the buying party (here, the counterparty if it is the buyer) by permitting recovery of first-dollar losses once the threshold is met. Per the controlling deal-team instruction, the CLIENT WILL CONCEDE the basket conversion. No further negotiation is required on this discrete point.
• Silent Cap Reduction. Distinct from the basket mechanics, the counterparty silently reduces the overall indemnification cap. Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift to our client. Because the cap is being reduced at the same time Schedule 5.2 confirms a set of retained liabilities remain with the counterparty, the net effect is to depress the ceiling of recovery for any indemnifiable losses while leaving the liability-shifting risk asymmetric in the counterparty's favor. The markup gives no corresponding concession.

Recommendation: ACCEPT the basket conversion (concede, per the controlling instruction), but REJECT the silent reduction of the indemnification cap. Counter with language restoring the firm-standard cap, noting that Schedule 5.2's retained liabilities must not be under-secured by a reduced cap. This counter is a value/risk asymmetry point rather than a walk-away point, but it should not be conceded absent reciprocal relief.

DEVIATION 2 — Material Adverse Effect: New Carve-Outs for Regulatory Action

What the Markup Does. The Counterparty Markup adds carve-outs to the definition of "Material Adverse Effect" for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter."

Analysis.
• Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries. These pending inquiries intersect precisely the new MAE carve-outs. Because the scheduled exceptions control over the general statements in the base materials, and because the newly drafted carve-outs are tailored to remove the very regulatory exposure that Schedule 3.7 flags as live, the carve-outs would operate to strip the client of MAE protection for the exact risk identified on the schedules.
• This is a targeted, deal-sourced deviation rather than a neutral market-standard drafting preference. The carve-outs are crafted to carve out the specific matter's regulatory risk, functionally neutralizing the MAE safety valve for that risk.

Recommendation: REJECT the MAE carve-outs. The carve-outs should, at most, be narrowed to general, non-matter-specific regulatory carve-outs that do not swallow the schedule 3.7 exposure. Where the counterparty insists, counter that any regulatory carve-out must exclude the specific pending inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7 and must not defeat MAE protection for those disclosed liabilities.

DEVIATION 3 — Limitation Period: Shortened Survival of the Core Representations

What the Markup Does. The Counterparty Markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival of the core representations.

Analysis.
• Exhibit B sets the survival matrix for the agreement. The markup's limitation-period change directly contradicts the survival matrix in Exhibit B by shortening the survival window for the core representations.
• The controlling deal-team instruction is unambiguous: the client treats any survival-period reduction as a WALK-AWAY ISSUE. This is a red line. It is the single highest-priority point in the engagement and is not negotiable.

Recommendation: REJECT the survival-period reduction categorically. This deviation is a WALK-AWAY issue per the controlling instruction. We should insist on the survival matrix in Exhibit B and decline to move forward unless the survival periods for the core representations are preserved. No counter is appropriate on this point; the markup must be withdrawn on this element.

IV. PRIORITIZED RECOMMENDATION SUMMARY

| # | Deviation | Recommendation | Priority |
|---|-----------|----------------|----------|
| 1a | Basket conversion (deductible → tipping) | ACCEPT (concede) | Low — conceded |
| 1b | Silent reduction of indemnification cap | REJECT / COUNTER | Medium |
| 2 | MAE carve-outs for regulatory action | REJECT / narrow | High |
| 3 | Survival-period reduction for core reps | REJECT — WALK-AWAY | Critical / red line |

V. CONCLUSIONS AND NEXT STEPS

The Counterparty Markup is largely consistent with firm-standard position but advances three material departures. Two are resolvable through targeted negotiation: the silent cap reduction (counter with restoration of the firm-standard cap, mindful of Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities) and the MAE carve-outs (reject or narrow so they do not capture the Schedule 3.7 pending regulatory inquiries). One is a deal-critical red line: the survival-period reduction, which the client treats as a walk-away issue and which contradicts Exhibit B's survival matrix; this must be rejected outright.

We recommend returning a markup that (i) concedes the basket conversion as instructed, (ii) restores the indemnification cap and preserves Schedule 5.2 liability allocation, (iii) removes or narrowly reframes the MAE regulatory carve-outs so they do not capture the disclosed Schedule 3.7 inquiries, and (iv) deletes the shortened survival period in favor of the Exhibit B matrix. If the counterparty holds firm on the survival-period reduction, the engagement should be treated as at a walk-away impasse per the controlling instruction.

Prepared for further counsel review and client approval prior to circulation of a counter-markup consistent with the above.

[End of Memorandum]
